The **Eiffel Tower** is a wrought-iron lattice tower in Paris, France, built by Gustave Eiffel's company for the 1889 World's Fair. It was completed in two years (1887–1889) and originally intended as a temporary structure. Standing about 330 meters tall, it's one of the world's most recognizable landmarks and a symbol of France — nicknamed *La Dame de Fer* ("The Iron Lady"). What started as a controversial design is now Paris's most-visited paid monument.

The **Eiffel Tower** is a wrought-iron lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, named after engineer **Gustave Eiffel**. It was built by his company between **1887 and 1889** as the centerpiece of the 1889 World's Fair.

Originally criticized by some artists and intellectuals, it was meant to be temporary — but it stuck around. At **330 meters** tall (1,083 ft), it was the world's tallest structure until the Chrysler Building in 1930. Today it's the most-visited paid monument in the world and pretty much the universal symbol of Paris.
